metadata.title: Megjegyzesek egy versenyfeladathoz (Remarks on a competition problem)
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced. Paper is in Hungarian with Russian and German abstracts.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: metadata.json lists this as 'On Maximal Paths and Circuits of Graphs' by Erdos & Gallai (1959), but the actual PDF is 'Megjegyzesek egy versenyfeladathoz' by Erdos & Suranyi (1959), a Hungarian paper on a number-theoretic divisibility problem from a math competition.

nodes.name: Gallai's divisibility selection problem
nodes.statement: Given distinct positive integers $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_n$ and any $a_n$ consecutive integers, how many must be selected so that their product is always divisible by $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$?
nodes.statement_clean: Determine the minimum number of integers to select from any block of $a_n$ consecutive integers so that their product is divisible by the product of the given integers.

nodes.name: Schweitzer competition problem (n=3 case)
nodes.statement: Decide: (a) For positive integers $a > b$, do any $b$ consecutive integers contain two whose product is divisible by $ab$? (b) For positive integers $a < b < c$, do any $c$ consecutive integers contain three whose product is divisible by $abc$?
nodes.statement_clean: The n=2 and n=3 specializations of Gallai's problem, posed at the 1954 Schweitzer competition.
nodes.origin_citation: Schweitzer Miklos Mathematical Memorial Competition 1954, problem 6

nodes.name: Counterexample for the n=3 case
nodes.statement: With $a = 7 \cdot 11$, $b = 7 \cdot 13$, $c = 11 \cdot 13$, the interval of consecutive integers $[6 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 - 71, 6 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 71] = [5935, 6077]$ contains no three integers whose product is divisible by $abc$.
nodes.statement_clean: An explicit counterexample showing the answer to part (b) of the competition problem is negative.

nodes.name: Reduced parametrization for n=3
nodes.statement: For three integers $a, b, c$ with $(a,b,c) = d$, write $a = a_1 d$, $b = b_1 d$, $c = c_1 d$ with $(a_1, b_1, c_1) = 1$. Set $u = (a,b)/d$, $v = (a,c)/d$, $w = (b,c)/d$ (pairwise coprime), and write $a = a' u v d$, $b = b' u w d$, $c = c' v w d$ with $a', b', c'$ pairwise coprime.
nodes.statement_clean: A canonical decomposition of three integers into a common factor $d$ and pairwise-coprime parts.

nodes.name: Sufficient condition for three-element selection
nodes.statement: If three multiples of $a, b, c$ found in the consecutive block are not all the same number, then either three distinct multiples of $a$, $b$, $c$ exist in the block, or one can construct three integers whose product is divisible by $[a,b] \cdot [(a,b),c] \cdot ((a,b),c) = abc$.
nodes.statement_clean: Whenever the standard multiples of $a$, $b$, $c$ in the block are not collapsed to a single integer, three integers can be chosen with product divisible by $abc$.
assumptions: $a, b, c$ are distinct positive integers
the consecutive block has length equal to $\max(a,b,c)$
conclusions: three integers in the block can be selected whose product is divisible by $abc$

nodes.name: Necessary structure for counterexamples (n=3)
nodes.statement: A counterexample requires that there exists $k$ in the block divisible by $a$, $b$, and $c$, with no other multiple of any of $a, b, c$ in the block; in particular $\max(a,b,c) < 2 \min(a,b,c)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A counterexample to the n=3 problem can only occur when there is a single integer divisible by all three, and the largest of the three is less than twice the smallest.
assumptions: $a, b, c$ are distinct positive integers
the block of $\max(a,b,c)$ consecutive integers contains no three whose product is divisible by $abc$
conclusions: there exists $k$ in the block with $a \mid k$, $b \mid k$, $c \mid k$
no other multiple of $a$, $b$, or $c$ lies in the block

nodes.name: Refined structural conditions on counterexample
nodes.statement: In a counterexample to the n=3 problem one must have $a' = b' = c' = 1$, the parameters $u, v, w$ are distinct primes with $\max(u,v,w) < 2 \min(u,v,w)$, and $k$ is not divisible by the square of any of $u, v, w$.
nodes.statement_clean: The reduced decomposition forces $u, v, w$ to be primes within a factor of 2, and the special integer $k$ to be squarefree with respect to them.

nodes.name: Theorem I: Complete characterization of counterexamples (coprime case)
nodes.statement: Let $a < b < c$ be coprime positive integers. There exist $c$ consecutive integers from which no 3 can be selected with product divisible by $abc$ iff $a = uv$, $b = uw$, $c = vw$ for primes $u < v < w < 2u$. The block must contain an integer whose gcd with $abc$ is $uvw$, but no other multiple of $a$ and no multiple of $w^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: When $(a,b,c)=1$, counterexamples exist exactly when $a, b, c$ have the form $uv, uw, vw$ for primes $u<v<w<2u$, with structural conditions on the special block element.
assumptions: $a < b < c$ are positive integers with $(a,b,c) = 1$
conclusions: counterexample exists iff $a = uv$, $b = uw$, $c = vw$ for primes $u<v<w<2u$
block must contain $k$ with $\gcd(k, abc) = uvw$ and no other multiple of $a$ and no multiple of $w^2$ in the block

nodes.name: Smallest counterexample triple
nodes.statement: The triple $(a,b,c) = (7 \cdot 11, 7 \cdot 13, 11 \cdot 13)$ gives the smallest counterexample, since $7$ is the smallest prime followed by two primes less than its double. A second example: $(143, 187, 221) = (11 \cdot 13, 11 \cdot 17, 13 \cdot 17)$ with the block $[2313, 2533]$ avoiding multiples of $17^2 = 289$ around $2431 = 11 \cdot 13 \cdot 17$.
nodes.statement_clean: Theorem I yields the original counterexample as smallest, and a further explicit family from primes $11, 13, 17$.

nodes.name: Theorem II: Selection of 4 always suffices for n=3
nodes.statement: If $a < b < c$ are positive integers and one is given any $c$ consecutive integers, then there always exist at most 4 of them whose product is divisible by $abc$.
nodes.statement_clean: Even without the coprimality assumption, four integers from any block of $c$ consecutive integers always suffice to obtain a product divisible by $abc$.
conclusions: in any $c$ consecutive integers there exist at most $4$ whose product is divisible by $abc$

nodes.name: Theorem III: Sufficient block length $\sqrt{2}\, c$ for 3-selection
nodes.statement: If $\alpha \geq \sqrt{2}$, then from any $\alpha c$ consecutive integers one can select 3 whose product is divisible by $abc$. If $\alpha < \sqrt{2}$, there exist $a < b < c$ and a block of $\alpha c$ consecutive integers in which the assertion fails.
nodes.statement_clean: The threshold for guaranteed 3-element selection from a block proportional to $c$ is exactly $\sqrt{2}\, c$.
conclusions: if $\alpha \geq \sqrt{2}$ then 3 integers in the block have product divisible by $abc$

nodes.name: Theorem IV: Counterexamples exist for every $k \geq 3$
nodes.statement: For every $k \geq 3$ there exist $k$ distinct positive integers and a block of consecutive integers (of length equal to the largest of them) such that no $k$ of the consecutive integers have product divisible by the product of the given $k$ integers.
nodes.statement_clean: Counterexamples to Gallai's question exist for all $n \geq 3$.
conclusions: there exist $k$ distinct positive integers and a block of $\max$-many consecutive integers such that no $k$-subset of the block has product divisible by the product of the given integers

nodes.name: Lower bound: nearly $2n$ selections may be needed
nodes.statement: There exist $l$ primes $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_l$ with $2 p_1 > p_l^2$ such that the products $p_i p_j$ for $i,j = 1,\ldots,l$ (so $n = l(l+1)/2$ given numbers) require at least $l(l-1) + 1 \approx 2n$ selections from a suitable block to make the product divisible by the product of the given numbers.
nodes.statement_clean: For some configurations of $n = l(l+1)/2$ given integers, almost $2n$ selections are required, showing the answer can be far worse than $n+1$.

nodes.name: The function $f(n)$
nodes.statement: $f(n)$ is the smallest number such that, for any $n$ distinct positive integers $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_n$, from any $f(n)\, a_n$ consecutive integers one can select $n$ integers including a multiple of each $a_i$, with distinct $a_i$ assigned to distinct multiples.
nodes.statement_clean: $f(n)$ measures how long a block (in units of $a_n$) is needed to find a system of distinct representatives of multiples of the $a_i$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on $f(n)$ via Erdos 1935
nodes.statement: For some constants $a, c > 0$, $f(n) \geq c (\log n)^a$. In particular $f(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: $f(n)$ grows at least like a power of $\log n$.

nodes.name: Upper bound $f(n) \leq C' \sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement: There exists a constant $C' > 0$ such that $f(n) \leq C' \sqrt{n}$.
nodes.statement_clean: $f(n)$ grows at most like a constant times $\sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: External: Erdos 1935 on integers without divisor in $[n,2n]$
nodes.statement: The number of positive integers up to $x$ having no divisor in $[n, 2n]$ is less than $x / (\log n)^a$ for a constant $a > 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Cited density estimate used to prove the lower bound on $f(n)$.
nodes.origin_citation: P. Erdos, Note on sequences of integers no one of which is divisible by any other, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935), 126-128

nodes.name: $\sqrt{n}$ multiples in length $2 a_n$
nodes.statement: From any $2 a_n$ consecutive integers one can select pairwise distinct multiples of at least $\sqrt{n}$ different $a_i$'s.
nodes.statement_clean: Any block of length $2 a_n$ contains at least $\sqrt{n}$ distinct $a_i$ assigned distinct multiples.
conclusions: at least $\sqrt{n}$ pairwise distinct multiples of distinct $a_i$ can be chosen from the block

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem I
nodes.statement: Combine the structural propositions PrP348.1, PrP348.2, PrP348.3 to identify counterexamples; then show that when $a = uv$, $b = uw$, $c = vw$ with $u<v<w<2u$ primes, an explicit block can be constructed avoiding multiples of $w^2$ near a multiple of $uvw$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem II
nodes.statement: Drop the coprimality assumption; the analysis of section 4 still produces a $k$-tom multiple plus three further distinct multiples of $ud$, $vd$, $wd$ giving four selected integers with product divisible by $abc$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III
nodes.statement: Show $\alpha c \geq \min(2 a, w^2 d)$ suffices via case analysis, and that $\alpha < \sqrt{2}$ admits configurations $u, v, w$ with $w$ near $\sqrt{2} u$ and consecutive primes giving counterexamples.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem IV
nodes.statement: Modify the section 1 counterexample for $3 \leq k \leq 12$ by selecting from $13, 2 \cdot 13, \ldots, 11 \cdot 13$ along with $7 \cdot 11$; for $k > 12$ use sufficiently large primes $u < v < w < 2u$ obeying the conditions of Theorem I.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem V (lower bound $\geq 2n$)
nodes.statement: Choose $l$ primes with $2 p_1 > p_l^2$, form the $l(l+1)/2$ products $p_i p_j$, and exhibit a block where any selection requires $l(l-1)+1$ elements.

nodes.name: Proof of $f(n) \leq C' \sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement: Iteratively select $\sqrt{n}$ multiples per block of length $2 a_n$ via Lemma LP348.1; sum the geometric-like series of selections to bound the number of iterations $l$ and conclude $f(n) \leq C' \sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Iteration setup
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma LP348.1 to obtain at least $\sqrt{n}$ distinct $a_i$ assigned multiples in a block of length $2 a_n$.

nodes.name: Recurse on remaining $a_i$
nodes.statement: Repeat on the remaining $n_1 = n - k \leq n - \sqrt{n}$ numbers using the next adjacent block of length $2 a_n$, selecting $\sqrt{n_1}$ further multiples; continue until all $a_i$ are assigned.

nodes.name: Bound iteration count by partial-square-root summation
nodes.statement: Let $n_0 = n$, $n_{r+1} = n_r - \sqrt{n_r}$; bound the number of iterations $l$ by partitioning indices $r$ by the size of $\sqrt{n_r}$ relative to $x = \sqrt{n}/2^s$ to obtain $l \leq 3 \sqrt{n} + S \leq C \sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Conclude $f(n) \leq C' \sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement: Since each iteration uses a block of length $2 a_n$ and there are at most $C \sqrt{n}$ iterations, $f(n) \leq C' \sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Proof of $f(n) \geq c (\log n)^a$
nodes.statement: Take $a_i$ as the integers in $[n, 2n]$; partition $[1, x]$ into segments of length $f(n) \cdot 2n$; if each contained $n$ chosen multiples of distinct $a_i$, the count of multiples of integers in $[n, 2n]$ up to $x$ would exceed the bound from Theorem TP348.8, giving $f(n) \geq c (\log n)^a$.

nodes.name: Tight bounds for $f(n)$
nodes.statement: Both the lower bound $c (\log n)^a$ and the upper bound $C' \sqrt{n}$ on $f(n)$ appear loose; determine the true asymptotic order of $f(n)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Close the gap between the polylogarithmic lower bound and the square-root upper bound on $f(n)$.

nodes.name: Tight constant in lower bound for selection count
nodes.statement: Is the worst-case number of integers needed to select from a block to make their product divisible by the product of the given $n$ integers asymptotically $(2 - \epsilon) n$, or can it be even larger?
nodes.statement_clean: Determine whether the constant 2 in Theorem TP348.5 is tight.

nodes.name: Both bounds appear loose
nodes.statement: Both the lower bound (counting all multiples of all $a_i$) and the upper bound (estimating distinct multiples in a block of length $2 a_n$) on $f(n)$ are noted as crude.
